sentences.text: I am.
Wow.
This meeting is being recorded.
How long have you been there?
21 years.
Oh, wow.
So you're not one of these new guys?
I am not one of the new ones.
I've just turned up.
No, it's getting expensive there now.
Is there lots of people moving into all of the apartments?
Yeah, just I think from, from COVID everyone went to villas and then there was a huge rush of new villa destinations getting built around and outside of Dubai.
And then Ukraine and Russia happened and they all turned up with lots of, lots of cash and bags and sent apartment and villas and, and cars and everything just was skyrocketed.

It's coming down a little bit now, but it's, I mean we're five years later and I mean some villas that are going for rent nowadays are just ridiculous, ridiculously priced and either it's big, big organizations are paying for CEOs etc.
Etc.
To move into those as a rented or lots of new money coming into market, lots of cryptos and all that kind of stuff.

So yeah, it's, yeah, it's definitely changing which is, it's a shame because it kind of out prices a lot of, you know, when you look at the team that you have and you know the salaries that they pay, they kind of have to live a little bit further away.
But if, you know, most of the guys are from the uk, they're used to traveling, you know, they're used to getting the metro, the bus or driving into to an office.
So what used to be a 10, 15 minute car journey now with traffic is just an hour long.
Wow.
God.
So it's busy.
So what took you there 25 years ago?
Because that's when it was just all desert.
Yeah, it was, it was all desert.
I, I came out to work for Heineken, was a Heineken brand manager.
So previous to that I, I worked in the drinks industry in, in Scotland, predominantly working on Stella and tenants Lager, doing a lot of the festivals.
And then, you know, I was 24 at the time and my father just passed away and I decided I'm going to travel, I'm going do what he did.
He, he traveled and I was born in Brazil and I thought let's, let's see what's out there.
And then Heineken was the ones who flew me out.
So I applied for two jobs.
One New York for Glenn Fiddick and one for Heineken.
And by the time I got to the airport I got an offer from Heineken and then I thought I'll do two years, as most expats back then did.
And yeah, 21 years later, I'm.
I'm here and I started my business 18 years ago.
Jesus, what a story.
That's amazing.
Yes, it's, it's interesting right now in the uk because everybody is, is looking to Dubai as one of the other choices.
So it used to be sort of Australia or.
Yeah.
They were looking at places like Portugal.
But everybody's talking about Dubai now and this new push with the no tax or tax free sounds that they're doing.
I think, you know what, it's.
You get a whole host of different types of bodies moving out.
You know, a lot of people have come out who were recycle engineers, let's call them that, or gardeners or plumbers, who are now selling multi million pound properties on the Palm.
So you've got a lot of real estate guys, you know, when previously it used to be finance brokerage, you know, like the, the likes of De Veers trying to sell.
You get your pension at the uk.
So it's all kind of changed into real estate market is, is huge.
I mean, the guys above us house and house, they have got a huge amount of footprint in this complex that we're in.
Yeah.
I've got friends of mine who owns real estate businesses and he started at the same time as I did.
We used to play football together and now he's just bought himself a private jet.
Brilliant.
So, well, there, there's definitely success stories and then there's other stories of people not making it.
But.
Yeah, you know, I think I was reading an article about the amount of millionaires moving out of the UK to Dubai and, and because everyone speaks English.
Yep.
You know, so you don't need to learn Spanish or Portuguese or, you know, everyone, everyone speaks English.
And what's it like culturally?
Because I did go to Dubai a few years ago, but I found like, kind of Arab guys just do their own thing.
There's pretty much like.
There would seem to be no mix.
We were at the Rugby Sevens.
Yeah.
Obviously attracts a British audience anyway.
But, um, it just.
Yeah, just my entire sort of trip was completely separate.
Yeah, no, it is, it is a.
It is quite separate.
I think if you're new coming into market, very rarely will you come across an Emirati.
I think because I've been here for such a long time, I've got Emirati friends.
But nowadays I think it's from a cultural mix.
Know, there's, there's so much options.

I mean, my wife, as an Example, she plays paddle and she plays with Sheikha Latifa, one of his Royal Highness's daughters, you know, so it, it, it's, it's funny where I think because we've been here for such a long time, we don't see that as, as anything.
Yeah, yeah.
So long.
Yeah.
I guess it's like playing with Prince Harry.
That's, that's the relationship that would never happen anywhere else in the world, you know, but my wife is friends with the shaker's daughter and plays paddle with her and.
But you know, when, if I speak to anyone in the agency, you know, do you hang around with any of the Emirates or Arabs and they're like, no.
Yeah.
You know, so I think there's this real.

I think if you've been here for a long time, you know, culturally, how to engage and be friends with people and, you know, I think it's, yes, it's, it's a lot harder for the new, the newbies coming over to engage.
Otherwise, you know, the expat community becomes your family.
Yeah, no, I found that we were in LA for six months, funnily enough.
Like the amount of English people that want to hang out with you, it's annoying because you want to meet America.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, absolutely.
Like constantly people like wanted to take for a coffee and stuff and.
Yeah, it becomes exactly difficult.
I was in la.
We were setting up, we were setting up a business in LA just before COVID Unfortunately, we never got through the, the visa situation as Trump kind of blocked everything.
But I was the same.
All my friends in LA were expats.
No one was actually born in the us.
I had Italian friends, British friends, Australian friends, but no actual LA born and bred.
It was just very hard to kind of break into that kind of.
Unless you had something for them, you know.
Yeah, it's peculiar, isn't it?
It is peculiar.
I found it really, really odd.
Even the American guy that lived next door turned out to be a British guy that been there 30 years.
So how about you?
You've been doing capsule A for a while.
Yeah, I should, I should tell you about myself and what we're doing.
So, yeah, we are, we are capital A group.
We've been around for about seven, eight years and we, we are an M A advisory initially.

So we've been working with either founders of larger agencies or ambitious agencies that are looking to bolt on, you know, businesses or working with private equity and investors, private investors who have built agency groups as well.
So we've been, the people have gone out and found the businesses and brought them in.
Yeah.
But this year we are launching our own roll up.
We're in the late stages with a couple of businesses.
We've been working particularly recently on a.
A bunch of deals with a company called Skyview in the States which gave us.
We've done four acquisitions with these guys.
One isn't announced but, but they're rebranded as Hovercraft.
I don't come across across Hovercraft, but great, great agency.
But off the back of that we, we are now just building our own.
It's a very similar type of roll up.
We've learned a lot as we've.
We've gone along and we've seen the, the growth in the immersive space in particular.
So brand experiences are the new thing.
OB that was a big thing that brands wanted to switch from just sending digital messages to people to actually immersing people in a brand experience.
And I don't think that'll even go away if we do have another lockdown scenario.
I think brands understand the power of that interaction.
So all I can see is an upward curve with that kind of thing.
And what we're seeing is a huge amount of investment from private equity as well.
It's always kind of been there for marketing services, but certainly the last five years or so private equity has seen that you can't really mess up.
Yeah.
Investments in, in marketing because it's just so, it's just so sort of diverse.
I mean there are so many companies.
I see it like almost like record labels signing up new artists.
Every time you sign somebody up, that's great.
But there's always a new sort of change in how marketing's done.
There's new technology and then there's the young kids that come along and they split off from the agency that they were in.
And you know, it's kind of like that, isn't it?
So there's constantly new stuff to sign.
Private equity really get that.

So what we're looking to build is a group of five to eight immersive, experiential and event businesses and then grow that organically over a period of time, short period of time hopefully, and then exit to PE again a second time.
So we're looking at a sort of story arc starting this year to about 3, 3 years onto 26, which would take us to about 2029 and then exit the business.
I haven't done this a couple of times now.
It's kind of second sense sort of thing to.
So what we're looking for.
So we do have a really good agency business that we want to build on which we're hopefully just about to close in the next month or so.
But what we're looking for is really immersive companies that have got great experience with brands.
So because the events company we've got is more about large scale events and less about the engagement with brands.
They've got all the ops side of things but not really.
Not really the brand clients that we're looking for to.
To build outwards.
Yeah.
Are they UK based?
They are UK based, yeah.
So they're in the UK and us.
They're just building out their US business.
So they've been in the US about two, three years.
They're kind of like the.
The company in the uk.
Okay.
Looking to replicate that in the us.
Yeah.
But I'd love to hear more about light blue and really what it is that you're looking to do because obviously I don't know how long you've been going.
What did you say?
18, 18 years as light blue.
Light blue, yeah.
That's amazing.
I mean that's a long.
That's a long history.
But it'll be.
Be interesting to know what it is that you're looking to achieve.
Is.
Is there an exact timeline for you and.
No, I mean look, we've always been quite fiercely independent.
I sit on the board of Tribe Global which is an independ agencies so I've always been a bit of a champion for independency.
We have been approached a number of times over the 18 years that we've been on the go and I guess, you know, we've, you know, you win awards, whatever people think about awards.
I'm not a massive fan of it but it is what it is.
You know.
We were campaign experiential agency of the year Middle east, two years in the row.
We then took last year off and then we've been shortlisted just today for.
For this year.
We were a couple years ago we were approached by a independent group.
Pretty much sounds very similar to what you're trying to achieve and we had good conversations with them.
They wanted me to.

To roll in with one of their existing agencies which I didn't see that a huge issue with but they wanted me to, to head up global experience for their agency across Paris, London and New York and la, which would have been quite interesting and I think it just didn't work out.
You know when you.
I think from a.
A click perspective.
I met the owner of the agency a couple of times in New York.
And I got on with him very well.
But I think the.
The leadership and the kind of direction wasn't really where we wanted and what we wanted.
So we kind of.
I mean, we had a call option in place, but that was.
And then we.
We kind of just moved away from the conversation.

And then more recently, again, we've been approached by a very big business who have a huge amount of different arms to their business, which was very interesting for us because they were kind of looking for us from a creative perspective to come in and really ramp up.
And we're actually.
We're still doing work with them as we speak, winning business for them as a kind of a white label.
And we've actually partnered up on a pitch as well to a Saudi client who's actually both our clients.
So.
Yeah, so.
But we've never.
I've never set the business up for a sale.
So, you know, the business is very much.
It's.
I own the business 100.
It kind of, to a certain level, kind of funds the lifestyle that we have, rather than thinking about the Etaba and leaving cash in and all that kind of stuff.
But I think the reality of us moving forward as a business and growing the business, you know, we're.

We fly in and out.

So we've actually.

Yeah.

But so do you mean that you always have to work with another agency.
And you, you're kind of sometimes yeah.

We work very well with them.
We know Monks.

So we, we, we play quite nicely with other agencies.

And he, and he wanted to meet us.
So we had breakfast and it was possibly the strangest breakfast.

And then he was just like, that's very hard business.
Experiential, very hard business.
How can you forecast?
I'm like, well that's tough.

Right.

Long term.

Getting more of the.

Yeah, something like that.

Dollars?
Yeah, yeah, dollars.

Okay.

Have you managed to stay profitable through.

Wow.

Yeah.

Right.

Is that.

Yeah.

So.

People.

No worries.

summary.overview:
- **Dubai Real Estate Surge:** Villa and apartment prices are soaring due to wealthy buyers, impacting local commuting and employee choices.  
- **Revenue Challenges:** Light Blue's revenue plateaued at $15M, attributed to strategic shifts and market disruptions affecting large project focus.  
- **Profitability Issues:** Margins dropped from 46% to break-even; external factors like the Gaza conflict affected UAE client budgets.  
- **Acquisition Interest:** Light Blue received multiple acquisition offers but remains independent, prioritizing cultural fit and leadership alignment.  
- **Growth Vision:** Expansion into the UK and enhanced investment needed to access larger brands and capital for significant projects.  
- **Next Steps for Collaboration:** Both parties to sign NDA and share financials to evaluate potential partnership or acquisition opportunities.
summary.short_summary: The discussion highlighted the significant rise in Dubai's real estate prices driven by wealthy buyers, impacting local commuting and employee choices. David Balfour shared insights on Light Blue's challenges, including a revenue plateau of $15 million, profitability issues due to market disruptions, and a strategic shift towards larger projects requiring substantial cash flow. The agency has remained independent despite multiple acquisition offers, emphasizing the importance of cultural fit. Future growth plans involve expanding into the UK, seeking investments to access larger brands, and enhancing project capabilities. There is also a rising interest from private equity in immersive marketing services, presenting potential collaboration opportunities for Light Blue with Capital A Group, which could enhance its market positioning and project scale.
